overview: Acho Dene Koe is a living Dene First Nation centred at Fort Liard. Its traditional territory and waters extend across the Northwest Territories, British Columbia and Yukon, with relationships to François Lake as well. Modern jurisdictional boundaries do not encompass the whole of this homeland.

periods.title: Mission and colonial change
periods.summary: The Fort Liard mission was established in 1859. Missionaries and the Grey Nuns influenced local craft designs, while communities maintained hunting, fishing, trapping and gathering.

periods.title: The Fort Liard treaty relationship
periods.summary: Fort Liard representatives signed an adhesion to Treaty 11 in July 1922. This local event followed the main treaty negotiations of the previous year.

periods.title: Craft work and a local market
periods.summary: Acho Dene Native Crafts began in 1976. Its Fort Liard enterprise links household producers with customers for baskets, footwear, jewellery and other work.

periods.title: Community priorities and cultural teaching
periods.summary: The Nation’s 2024 wellness plan connects community well-being with language, land and intergenerational teaching. Its proposals include craft instruction and support for harvesters.

items.text: The Liard River serves different forms of travel across the year. Community knowledge describes canoes and other boats on open water, and dog teams on the frozen river. The same corridor connects fishing places, camps and neighbouring communities as its surface changes with the season.

Fish are eaten fresh, smoked or dried, and some catches feed working dogs. The seasonal account describes autumn storage in raised caches and winter net fishing through ice. Two survey participants also described distributing surplus fish to Elders, linking harvesting with responsibilities to other people.

The Nation’s 2021 study collected knowledge from five members through a survey adapted to pandemic restrictions. It recorded fishing practices and observations of environmental change to support future monitoring. These findings preserve named community knowledge without claiming to exhaust the Nation’s experience or establish every cause of change.

Fort Liard’s craft account describes selecting young, light-coloured spruce roots that bend without breaking easily. Long, straight roots reduce the number of joins needed in stitching. Their usefulness depends on choosing and preparing the material, not simply finding any root in the forest.

Makers split and peel the roots, soften them, and use flexible outer pieces for stitching. Prepared roots can be dried and moistened again when needed. This sequence turns a woodland material into a sewing element that can be stored and fitted to later work.

Birchbark basket making begins with a cut pattern and a prepared surface. Floral designs are laid out before damp quills are inserted through small awl holes. Decoration therefore forms part of a planned construction sequence, rather than an addition that can be placed anywhere without regard to the basket’s shape.

An inner bark lining, a sewn bottom and a split willow rim help form the container. A matching lid can be joined with moosehide strips. The published method includes sandpaper, a planer and clothespins, showing a living craft that combines inherited knowledge with available tools.

The Fort Liard craft enterprise, founded in 1976, sells work made by producers in the community. Its range includes birchbark baskets, moccasins, mittens and mukluks. The business connects household skill with income and visitors, while its products combine older techniques with modern materials.

The surviving Fort Liard treaty adhesion names Chief Thomas E. Kinla and two headmen alongside Commissioner Thomas William Harris. Dated 17 July 1922, it is a specific documentary trace of the encounter. Its existence does not mean that later disputes about land or the treaty’s meaning were resolved.

The Nation’s wellness plan describes the lasting effects of infectious disease and residential or boarding schools. It also records continued harvesting and community action. These accounts place cultural survival alongside serious colonial losses, rather than presenting either disruption or continuity as the whole story.

The 2024 plan proposes bringing Elders and young people together for sewing, hide tanning, tool making and community history. It also supports stories, language and land-based learning. These are stated priorities for passing knowledge on; the plan alone does not show that every proposed activity has already happened.

ending.text: Acho Dene Koe continues as a First Nation with a living homeland and community institutions. Treaty and land negotiations concern rights and government, not the disappearance of the people. The map’s 1500 endpoint is imported coverage, not a historical fall date.
